title: 74% of Indie Stores Are Invisible to ChatGPT Shopping. I Built an Open-Source Linter to Fix It (Gemma 2 + SerpApi)
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

Here is a quiet shift happening in e-commerce right now: buyers are stopping at ten blue links and asking ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, and Gemini directly:

"Find me breathable eucalyptus running shoes in US 10.5 under $120 in stock right now."

When an AI shopping agent crawls a big brand like Nike or Amazon, it reads pristine, server-rendered Schema.org JSON-LD microdata.

When that same AI agent crawls an independent Shopify store or D2C side hustle, it frequently hits a brick wall:

  1. Silent Variant Dropouts: Client-side JavaScript size/color pickers hide secondary SKUs from non-browser crawlers. The store has Size 10.5 in stock, but the root HTML only exposes Size 8.
  2. Missing Global Identifiers: Missing GTIN/UPC barcodes prevent AI agents from cross-verifying product authenticity across merchant registries.
  3. Price & Catalog Drift: Secondary reseller sites (Poshmark, eBay, Depop) outrank the official merchant on Google Shopping with outdated or undercut pricing.

Enterprise brands pay $2,000+/month for catalog observability platforms to catch these issues. Indie merchants and solo founders can't afford that.

So I built CatalogPulse — a fast, zero-install, open-source AI Commerce Linter that lets any merchant, freelancer, or agency audit a product URL in 10 seconds, cross-reference live market listings via SerpApi Google Shopping, and generate a validated, copy-pasteable Schema.org Product JSON-LD fix powered by Google Gemma 2.

title: PlxNative: A Fast Native Plex Client for LG webOS TVs, Built in Rust
summary:
Most smart-TV apps are web pages. On LG's webOS that usually means JavaScript running inside a browser engine, which then hands its output to a compositor before anything reaches the screen. PlxNative is a Plex client for LG webOS TVs that takes that layer out. Its developer, Gleb Linnik, writes in the README: "No Chromium, no JavaScript, no web view. It just draws."

This is an explainer, built from the project's README, its docs, its source and its release notes. I don't own an LG TV, so nothing here was tested on a real television. What I did run is the project's own Linux desktop simulator against its mock Plex server, and that section near the end shows exactly what that does and doesn't tell you.

What PlxNative is

  • An unofficial Plex client for LG webOS TVs. It is not made by or affiliated with Plex or LG; the project says so on its site and in TRADEMARKS.md.
  • Open source under GPL-3.0-or-later, © 2026 Gleb Linnik. The PlxNative name and brand artwork are excluded from the licence.
  • One person's project. The README calls it "one person's spare time".
  • Current release: v0.8.0, published on GitHub on 7 October 2026. Nightly builds already report 0.9.0-nightly.
  • Young and active. The repository was created on 3 July 2026, and when I checked on 16 October it had 969 stars and 95 forks, with commits landing the same morning.
  • Free. There's no paid tier. You need a Plex account and a Plex Media Server, and the FAQ confirms a free Plex server works.

Why it exists

The origin story is short. The developer's 2019 LG TV still had a great picture, but browsing a Plex library on it "felt slower than it needed to." Rather than tune a web app, he wrote a native one. In his words: "I use it every day to watch things off my server in the next room."

The site makes the argument with a pair of stacks. A typical TV app goes:

The app (a web page) -> JavaScript -> Browser engine -> Compositor -> OpenGL -> GPU -> Screen

PlxNative goes:

The app (native code) -> OpenGL -> GPU -> Screen

The claimed result is 60 fps on that 2019 set. I couldn't measure that, and the project itself says the simulator can't either. More on that below.

The architecture

Mostly Rust, with a thin C shell

The repository is overwhelmingly Rust. A rough line count on the current main gives about 576,000 lines of .rs files against about 7,300 lines of C and C++. That count includes tests and generated data, so treat it as a ratio, not a measure of features.

The structure is spelled out in rust-modules/Cargo.toml. It's a Cargo workspace whose root crate is linked into a small C app as a static library:

# Static library linked into the C app (hybrid migration): each ported module
# exposes the same C ABI its src/*.h declares, so the C code calls it unchanged.
[lib]
name = "plxnative_modules"

The workspace is split into layer crates: base, machine, net, platform, gfx, ui, plex, telemetry, data, session, media, appkit, screens and storage. docs/module-layers.md describes how they depend on one another.

A GPU-drawn interface

The UI goes through SDL2 and OpenGL ES (both are listed in the repo's topics), so there's no DOM and no layout engine. The design language is translucent "glass" panels over your own posters and backdrops, with text sized for reading across a room. The docs folder holds design notes on liquid glass, backdrop blur and a hardware budget for the glass effect, which gives a sense of how much of the work goes into making that look cheap enough for TV silicon.

Video on the TV's own decoder

Playback doesn't decode video in software. The README says the app "hands video to the same silicon the built-in apps use". In the code, that goes through a video-sink trait in the platform crate. On the TV it's implemented by a StarfishSink, which talks to LG's Starfish media APIs, and on the desktop by a HostSink.

What it can direct-play, per the README:

  • H.264 and HEVC, including 4K and 10-bit
  • Dolby Vision profiles 5 and 8
  • E-AC-3 with Atmos
  • AV1 or VP9 (10-bit VP9 only on webOS 4 sets), on TVs whose codec table lists that decoder

Anything else is transcoded by your Plex server. Before you press Play, the detail page shows whether a title will play directly or be converted on the server. The app also ships its own LGPL build of FFmpeg.

Features

From the README, the site and the 0.8.0 release notes:

  • Sign in on the TV by scanning a QR code with your phone, then pick a Plex Home profile. PIN-protected profiles are supported.
  • Browse your own and shared libraries, with Continue Watching, Recently Added, sort, filters (including unwatched-only) and an A–Z rail.
  • Search across every server you can reach, with results grouped by kind.
  • A full player with resume, seek and scrub, chapters, audio and subtitle tracks (image subtitles included), Skip Intro, Skip Credits, Up Next with auto-advance, and progress synced back to Plex.
  • New in 0.8.0: subtitle search from inside the player, ASS/SSA subtitles that keep their styling, browsing Plex collections, Boost dialog and Normalize loudness on servers with Plex Pass, a Settings section for playback, and Spanish and Belarusian translations.
  • Works without internet after the first sign-in. The app talks to your server directly, so the library keeps working on your home network when the internet is down.
  • Privacy defaults. Crash reports and usage analytics are two separate opt-in questions, both off until you say yes. The README says no title, search term, subtitle line, server name or address can appear in any report. The app talks to your Plex server, to plex.tv to sign in, and to discover.provider.plex.tv for cast biographies.

0.8.0 also changes one security behaviour. Some home servers only answer over plain HTTP. Earlier versions refused to send your Plex sign-in that way. 0.8.0 will connect, but only after asking "Connect without encryption?", and only for a server on the same network at a private address after every secure route, Plex's relay included, has failed.

How to install it

PlxNative isn't in the LG Content Store yet; the site says it's "in the process of review" with no confirmed date. There are two routes, and neither needs root.

Route 1: LG Developer Mode

The installation guide needs an LG TV on webOS 4.0 or newer, a Plex account with a server, and a Mac, Windows or Linux computer on the same network. In short:

  1. Create or sign in to an account on LG's developer site.
  2. Install the Developer Mode app on the TV, sign in, turn on Dev Mode Status (the TV restarts) and then Key Server.
  3. Note the TV's IP address and passphrase, and connect to it from webOS Dev Manager on your computer.
  4. Install the .ipk directly, or install Homebrew Channel first and get PlxNative from its catalogue.

For a manual download, verify the package first:

sha256sum -c ipk.sha256

The catch is renewal. Developer Mode sessions expire, and if one lapses LG removes the apps installed through it. The guide's advice is to open the Developer Mode app and press EXTEND before the remaining time runs out, with a calendar reminder. An expired session can't be extended.

Route 2: Homebrew Channel

If your TV already runs Homebrew Channel, open it, find PlxNative (a 19.6 MB download, listed as version 0.8.0) and select Install. Updates arrive there too, and the Channel checks the download's checksum before installing.

Nightlies

Adding https://plxnative.com/nightly/repo.json to Homebrew Channel installs PlxNative Nightly as a separate app with its own tile and sign-in. The README is blunt about these builds: "It is not tested on a television."

Limits and current status

The README has a section titled "The honest scope", and it's worth taking at its word:

  • Movies and TV shows only. No music, no photos, no Live TV or DVR.
  • No typing in server addresses. Servers come from your Plex account.
  • Relay and secure-only servers are supported but "haven't been watched end to end."
  • Not all TVs work. It needs webOS 4.0 or newer. A 2016 set on webOS 3.4.3 has been tested and works.

The known issues list is specific:

  • Some 2019 sets on LG's k5lp or k3lp chip, installed through Developer Mode, won't play video. The sandbox withholds a device the video path needs; Kodi and Moonlight hit the same wall. Without root there's no fix.
  • 2018 sets on webOS 3.9.3: sign-in and browsing work, but the prebuilt v0.8.0 never starts video (#249). A source build at or after commit 60f99c7 fixes it.
  • webOS 3.x restarts the stream on every seek instead of jumping in place.
  • Sets on the k6hp chip show a crash in opt-in reports that the developer can't reproduce without the hardware (#174).

Building the simulator on Linux

Since I couldn't put it on a TV, I built the desktop simulator the docs describe. The box runs Debian 13 on x86_64 with 8 vCPUs and no GPU. The only prerequisites were the SDL2, SDL2_ttf, Mesa, CMake and pkg-config dev packages plus a current stable Rust toolchain:

git clone https://github.com/GLinnik21/plx-native && cd plx-native
make sim-linux SIM_TDIR=rust-modules/target-sim

   Compiling plxnative-modules v0.8.0 (/workspace/plxnative/repo/rust-modules)
    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s) in 3m 08s
real    3m57.100s

That gave a 16 MB plxnative-sim binary on the first try. The extra 49 seconds went into fetching and building the libass stack (FreeType, FriBidi, HarfBuzz and friends).

The project's screenshot tool then boots the simulator against tests/mock_pms.py. That's a synthetic Plex server that also stands in for plex.tv, so no account, token or real library is involved. I ran it headless under Xvfb with software OpenGL:

python3 tools/demo_library.py derive
LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1 xvfb-run -a -s '-screen 0 1920x1080x24' \
  python3 tools/screenshots.py --bin rust-modules/target-sim/release/plxnative-sim \
  --out shots --only home-shelves,library-grid,search,detail,signin

Each scene settled in 2.2 to 4.9 seconds. One hiccup: the home scene also renders the website's link-preview card, and that step failed because the box lacked the file utility, so I captured home-shelves instead.

The sign-in screen is the QR flow, here pointed at the mock:

The Movies grid, with the sort and filter chips and the A–Z rail, browsing the project's demo library of openly licensed films:

And a title page, with the "Direct Play" label next to the runtime:

Be clear about what this proves. The simulator runs the same UI and Plex code as the TV build, and it boots, signs in to a fake server and draws every screen I asked for. But docs/building.md says plainly that it "cannot answer frame rate (different GPU), text rasterization, or anything about LG's decoder and video plane. Those need the set." The Linux build also has no video path at all; the Makefile notes that Play "intentionally reaches the host seam's existing 'no video path' result." So the speed and the hardware decoding, the two things PlxNative exists for, are still unverified by me.

Who it's for

If you run Plex at home and own a fairly recent LG TV, PlxNative is a well-documented alternative to the official app. Expect a project that tells you about its rough edges in the README. You'll need to be comfortable with Developer Mode renewals or Homebrew Channel until the LG Content Store listing lands. If you need music, Live TV or a set from the known-issues list, the README itself says the official app will serve you better.

If you're a developer, the repository is interesting on its own terms: a Rust UI stack drawing straight to GPU on TV-grade hardware, with design and performance notes for almost every decision. The simulator builds in a few minutes on plain Linux if you want to look around.

  • Site: https://plxnative.com/
  • Source: https://github.com/GLinnik21/plx-native

Open‑source automation could slash enterprise AI‑ops costs by up to 80 %—and it arrives this week.

Subtitle: A free, inspectable alternative to proprietary agents promises to reshape how companies automate GUIs, CLIs and vision‑driven tasks.

Lead – 15 Oct 2026

On 15 Oct 2026 the arXiv pre‑print 2610.22200 unveiled OpenGCUA, a fully open stack for general‑purpose computer‑use agents. Within 24 hours the repository earned 280 up‑votes on Hugging Face and was forked hundreds of times. The announcement matters because enterprises currently spend billions on closed agents that charge per‑action fees for GUI clicks, CLI commands and vision tasks. OpenGCUA offers the same capabilities without a pay‑per‑action bill and with complete source‑code transparency, challenging the business models behind GPT‑6 Astra, Microsoft Copilot for Windows and other proprietary stacks.

Quick‑Start Example: One Script, Three Platforms

A data‑science team needs to pull a daily sales report from a Windows‑only ERP, clean the CSV on a Linux server, and load the result into Snowflake. With OpenGCUA a single agent script replaces three separate RPA tools:

Step What the agent does

Act Sends the CSV through a CLI bridge that spawns a PTY on a Linux node, runs a Python transformer, and writes the cleaned file to a shared volume.
Authorize Requests a one‑click token from the team’s Slack‑integrated policy engine before uploading.
Complete Calls a Wasm‑based Snowflake plugin to push the payload; every action is logged via OpenTelemetry.

title: ScopeLock: open-weight AI that turns freelance scope creep into paid change orders
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

ScopeLock is a side-hustle tool for freelancers and small agencies who keep losing money to scope creep.

You paste your statement of work and a client thread (or import Slack JSON, or drop a voice memo). ScopeLock:

  • Labels each client ask as in-scope vs out-of-scope
  • Cites language from your SOW
  • Drafts a professional boundary reply
  • Runs a Side hustle cockpit: scope-creep score, TabPFN-estimated change-order hours, rush-fee math, and a client-ready change order you can export as Markdown

Who would pay? Solo devs, designers, and fractional engineers billing fixed-fee or milestone projects — anyone who needs receipts before saying yes to “just one more thing.”

Demo

Live app: https://scopelock.smriad.tech

Quick path on the demo: load samples → Index SOW → Analyze scope → open the change-order panel → Listen (ElevenLabs reads the suggested reply).

Production smoke test (Apple Sign-In creep sample): Mastra mode, high risk, TabPFN 15.3h, change-order ~$1,913 at $125/hr, voice MP3 generated, history stored in MongoDB.

curl -s https://scopelock.smriad.tech/api/health

smriad / scopelock

Local-first AI that turns freelance scope creep into paid change orders.

Built for Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle.

See docs/RENDER-SMRIAD.md.

  1. Deploy with render.yaml → service scopelock
  2. DNS: CNAME scopelock → *.onrender.com
  3. export RENDER_API_KEY=rnd_... && npm run sync:render (reads .env.local)

Local dev

cp .env.example .env.local   # fill partner keys
npm install
npm run dev

Optional: docker compose up -d for local pgvector; local Ollama for embeddings.

Open http://localhost:3000 — samples preloaded.

How it works

  1. Paste your statement of work and optionally Index into pgvector (embeds chunks with Ollama + stores in Postgres).
  2. Paste a client thread.
  3. Analyze scope — Ollama returns structured JSON: verdicts, SOW citations, reply draft, change-order line items.

If Ollama is offline, the app uses a demo analysis so you can still record a video (set DEMO_MODE=true on cloud hosts).

…

How I Built It

Open Gemma 3 (google/gemma-3-4b-it) is the reasoning core — on Render it runs via OpenRouter; locally you can point at Ollama instead. Mastra orchestrates the scope agent and workflow so analysis stays structured (verdicts, citations, reply, line items).

Agents Mastra agent + workflow

Tiger + Mongo keep SOW and analysis history under infrastructure you control — important when the product’s whole job is contractual evidence.

title: I built a photo and video editor that shows the maths behind every effect
summary:
Most editing apps give you a slider and hide what it does. I wanted one that shows the formula, so a beginner can see why an edit looks the way it does.
So I built Math Canvas: a photo and video editor that runs in your browser, in one HTML file. No sign-in and no uploads. Your files stay on your device.
Try it: https://www.cube3.in
Code (MIT): https://github.com/boya16573-design/Cube3.in
What it shows
Pick a layer and open the Check tab. You see the equations behind the look, for example how contrast works on linear light, or how a vignette fades toward the corners. You also get a quality test for your photo or video: resolution, sharpness, noise, exposure, colour balance and text contrast. When something fails, it shows the exact number and a one-tap fix.
Three details I enjoyed building

  1. Colour maths in linear light. Pixel values in a normal image are gamma-encoded, so averaging two pixels directly gives the wrong brightness. Averaging a black and a white pixel gives 128, but physically the result is closer to 188. Math Canvas converts to linear light with the exact sRGB formulas, does the blur, sharpen, glow and brightness maths there, and converts back.
  2. Lanczos resizing for exports. When you export at a larger size, photos are shrunk with a Lanczos-3 filter, again in linear light, instead of the browser's default.
  3. Frame-by-frame video export. The video exporter uses WebCodecs. It seeks each video to the exact time, draws the frame, encodes it, and writes the file, so no frames are dropped. Audio is mixed offline. It reports "420 of 420 frames rendered, 0 dropped". There's also a "Measure export error" button. It renders the preview and the real export, shrinks the export, and shows the RMSE and PSNR between them. In my tests the numbers came out around 47 to 52 dB, which means the two look the same. More maths It also draws graphs with derivatives and integrals, surfaces z = f(x, y), curves defined by F(x, y) = 0, and vector fields with divergence and curl. What it is not It doesn't use AI to make images. The "realistic scenes" and manga looks come from equations, so they are stylised, not photographs. MP4 export isn't tested in every browser. If it fails, it falls back to WebM. Heavy blur on a 4K image can be slow on older phones. Help wanted It's one file with no build step, which makes it easy to read and change. There are issues for new templates, graph presets, small-phone layout and testing MP4 in Safari and Firefox. Pull requests are welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.md in the repo. I'd love to hear what you think, and what bugs you find on your phone or browser.

  1. Colour maths in linear light. Pixel values in a normal image are gamma-encoded, so averaging two pixels directly gives the wrong brightness. Averaging a black and a white pixel gives 128, but physically the result is closer to 188. Math Canvas converts to linear light with the exact sRGB formulas, does the blur, sharpen, glow and brightness maths there, and converts back.
  2. Lanczos resizing for exports. When you export at a larger size, photos are shrunk with a Lanczos-3 filter, again in linear light, instead of the browser's default.
  3. Frame-by-frame video export. The video exporter uses WebCodecs. It seeks each video to the exact time, draws the frame, encodes it, and writes the file, so no frames are dropped. Audio is mixed offline. It reports "420 of 420 frames rendered, 0 dropped". There's also a "Measure export error" button. It renders the preview and the real export, shrinks the export, and shows the RMSE and PSNR between them. In my tests the numbers came out around 47 to 52 dB, which means the two look the same. More maths It also draws graphs with derivatives and integrals, surfaces z = f(x, y), curves defined by F(x, y) = 0, and vector fields with divergence and curl. What it is not It doesn't use AI to make images. The "realistic scenes" and manga looks come from equations, so they are stylised, not photographs. MP4 export isn't tested in every browser. If it fails, it falls back to WebM. Heavy blur on a 4K image can be slow on older phones. Help wanted It's one file with no build step, which makes it easy to read and change. There are issues for new templates, graph presets, small-phone layout and testing MP4 in Safari and Firefox. Pull requests are welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.md in the repo. I'd love to hear what you think, and what bugs you find on your phone or browser.

title: How LLMs are actually built — and why most "how it works" threads stop too early
summary:
Most "how LLMs work" explainers end at transformers and attention.

The parts that decide whether a model is actually good — the data pipeline, the post-training recipe, the evaluation setup, the systems work — usually get one sentence. Having watched a lot of talks on this, I wanted a version I could check rather than trust, so I turned Yann Dubois' Stanford CS229 guest lecture (Building Large Language Models, Summer 2024) into a small, timestamped reference.

It's now an installable agent skill, but the map is useful on its own. Here it is.

Five components, and who actually optimizes which

Component What it decides Who pushes it
Architecture capacity and shape academia
Training objective what "good" means during training academia
Data what the model has seen industry
Evaluation whether you can tell it improved industry
Systems whether training finishes at all industry

The uncomfortable conclusion from the lecture: architecture is where academic attention goes, and it's not where the practical leverage is.

Pretraining: compressing the internet

"Just train on the internet" hides the actual work. A real pipeline looks like this:

  1. Crawl — Common Crawl: ~250B pages, ~1 PB.
  2. Extract — HTML to text. Random pages are menus, footers, and truncated sentences.
  3. Filter — NSFW, harmful content, PII. Blacklists plus small classifiers.
  4. Dedupe — boilerplate, the same page under many URLs, paragraphs repeated thousands of times.
  5. Heuristics — odd token distributions, strange word lengths, too short, too long.
  6. Model-based filtering — train a classifier on sites linked from Wikipedia vs random web; prefer the former.
  7. Mix — up-weight code and books, down-weight entertainment. More code measurably helps reasoning.
  8. Final phase — high-quality data with a decaying learning rate; effectively overfitting on Wikipedia-grade text.

Team shape is worth noting: roughly 15 people on data in the Llama team, more people than on modelling, and more CPUs than GPUs.

On scale: loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute, which is why small runs can predict large ones. Chinchilla's takeaway is about 20 tokens per parameter — earlier models were typically data-starved.

Post-training: from autocomplete to assistant

SFT is next-token training on human-written ideal answers. The key insight: it teaches format and persona, not knowledge. LIMA scaled from 2,000 to 32,000 examples and quality barely moved. It also teaches the model to produce a plausible-looking answer instead of admitting ignorance — part of where hallucination comes from.

RLHF replaces demonstrations with preferences: show two answers, ask a human which is better, train a reward model (Bradley–Terry), then optimize the policy with PPO plus a penalty against over-optimizing the reward. Binary rewards are too sparse — you learn which answer won, not by how much.

DPO skips the RL loop: raise the likelihood of the preferred answer, lower the dispreferred one. Under standard assumptions the optimum matches PPO's, with a far simpler implementation, which is why it's now a default in open source.

The economics matter more than people think: humans agree with themselves only ~66% of the time on a binary preference task, human labels cost roughly $300 per 1,000 examples, and LLM labellers are about 50× cheaper with higher agreement with the human majority. The bias to watch: labellers prefer longer answers, so models trained on their preferences get verbose. That's why ChatGPT rambles.

Evaluation is where claims quietly break

  • Validation loss isn't comparable across PPO and DPO — different objectives.
  • Perplexity stops being meaningful after PPO: the model is a policy, not a distribution over text.
  • Chatbot Arena is the most trusted signal, and it's slow, expensive, and skewed toward technical users.
  • LLM-as-judge gets ~98% correlation with Arena for under $10 and under 3 minutes — with known biases toward length and its own family's style.

So before believing any benchmark number, ask three questions: which benchmark, against whom, judged by what.

Systems: the part nobody tweets about

Mixed precision (store weights in 32-bit, compute in 16-bit, update in 32-bit) and operator fusion (torch.compile gets roughly 2× faster training by moving data through GPU memory once instead of per op). Unglamorous, and often the difference between a training run finishing or not.

I packaged all of this as a skill file with a per-claim timestamp index, so you can verify instead of trusting my summary: github.com/lizhao888/llm-building-map (MIT).

Caveats, stated plainly: these are unofficial notes from a 2024 lecture, the speaker's hedges are preserved rather than upgraded to facts, and newer methods (long context, reasoning models, synthetic-data pipelines) are explicitly out of scope. Corrections welcome — especially where the field has moved on.

title: I poisoned 20 drug names to find out whether a local model belongs in a pharmacy
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

A prescription reader for a neighbourhood medical shop in India. It runs on the shop's own laptop, with no network connection at all.

The shopkeeper photographs a handwritten prescription. The system reads it, works out what was actually prescribed, and decides for itself which lines are safe to fill and which ones need a human to look at the paper.

The person who would pay for this is the chemist himself. He currently re-reads every prescription by hand because he cannot afford to get one wrong, and he is doing it at 9pm after a fourteen-hour day.

I should be upfront that the interesting part of this project is not the reading. It is the deciding when not to trust the reading.

Demo

The whole pipeline runs from one command on the shop's machine:

python3 scripts/run_page.py prescription.jpg

A synthetic page, end to end:

--- OCR (1.77s wall, 1.64s engine, 11 observations -> 9 lines) ---
  [conf 1.00] Dr. R.Deshmukh MBBSReg2019/4482
  [conf 1.00] Pt: Mr. Suresh Wankhede 42/M
  [conf 1.00] Ox: HTN, T2OM
  [conf 1.00] Rx
  [conf 1.00] 1. Tab Telma 40mg 1-0-0 x 30 days
  [conf 1.00] 2. Tab Glycomet GP2 1-0-1 x 30 days
  [conf 1.00] 3. Cap Pan 40 1-0-0 x15 days
  [conf 1.00] 4. Inj. Insulin 0-0-1 x 10 days
  [conf 1.00] Adv: review after 15 days

--- reconciled prescription (57.1s wall) ---
  diagnosis: HTN, T2DM
  [0] Telma 40mg Tab sig=1-0-0 days=30 conf=0.70
  [1] Glycomet GP2 Tab sig=1-0-1 days=30 conf=0.70
  [2] Pan 40 Cap sig=1-0-0 days=15 conf=0.60
  [3] Insulin Inj sig=0-0-1 days=10 conf=0.60

--- gate: review ---
  - line 1 (Telma): model confidence 0.70 is below 0.80
  - line 2 (Glycomet): model confidence 0.70 is below 0.80
  - line 3 (Pan): model confidence 0.60 is below 0.80
  - line 4 (Insulin): model confidence 0.60 is below 0.80

total: 58.9s (OCR 1.8s + model 57.1s)

Look at the third OCR line and then the diagnosis line underneath it. Those are the same characters read two different ways: the OCR returned Ox: HTN, T2OM, and the model worked out that it was Dx: HTN, T2DM. That is the one thing here the model does genuinely better than any regex I could write.

The other thing worth noticing is that on this page, every line goes to a human. That is entirely the confidence threshold, not the interesting checks, because the model was candid enough to score its own repairs at 0.60–0.70. The structural checks are what earn their place on the poisoned set further down, where the model is not candid and hands back 0.95 on answers that are wrong.

On the timing: 57s is the steady state. The first page after the model has been idle takes about 80s, because gemma3:4b has to be loaded into memory first. I have not tried to hide that number. On an eight-core laptop with no GPU it is the real price of not sending the page anywhere.

A hosted copy, and a precise list of what it does not do

parchi-hub8.onrender.com

I want to be exact about the limits of that link, because the limits happen to be the argument.

It replays the real recorded OCR transcript from the page above — not a mock-up of one, the actual Vision output, including the Ox: HTN, T2OM line. The gate, the reorder forecast and the Hindi counselling text all execute live against it. If you want to see the gate refuse something, it is the line 3 (Pan) entry in the "Why" column.

What it does not do is run gemma3:4b. Render's free tier is a Linux container with 512MB of RAM and no GPU, and the model is 3.4GB. So the reading step is a deterministic fixture, and the page says so on itself rather than pretending.

Two consequences, stated rather than left for you to find:

  • The forecast on that instance reports "method": "damped-mean", not TabPFN. Torch does not fit there either; requirements-ml.txt is what switches TabPFN on, and the fallback announces itself in that field — which is the whole reason the field exists.
  • There is no audio on that instance, deliberately. The speech works: demo/counselling-hindi.mp3 in the repo is a real render, 39 seconds of Hindi, checked in so you can listen without a key. But the key is not set on a public host, because an open endpoint that spends credits on every request is a bill that anyone who finds the URL can run up. The key stays on the shop's machine.

That last point is the project's own thesis turned back on itself, so it seemed like the wrong thing to make an exception for.

Code

github.com/kotewar/parchi

The pieces worth reading:

  • app/gate.py — the deterministic safety checks, including the two that mattered most
  • app/gemma.py — the local model call, with the two API gotchas commented so nobody re-breaks them
  • app/tabpfn_engine.py — refill forecasting from the shop's own dispense history
  • scripts/selfcheck.py — 53 regression checks, runnable with plain python3, no model, no setup
  • scripts/eval.py — the poisoned-name eval harness
  • data/eval_poisoned.json — the 20 test lines and their ground truth
  • eval_base_v2.json and eval_primed_v2.json — the two runs quoted below, committed so the claims are checkable

How I Built It

I started by trying to get a vision model to read the handwriting. That was the wrong instinct, and the community had already measured why: a dedicated OCR engine is roughly 300x faster than a general-purpose vision model at reading, with fewer character errors (The Dedicated OCR Engine Lost to the General Purpose Model by hexisteme).

So the architecture splits the job:

page image
   -> macOS Vision OCR        (reading: 1.8s/page)
   -> gemma3:4b via Ollama    (meaning: what is this medicine?)
   -> deterministic gate      (safety: may this be filled?)
   -> human review            (only what the gate refuses)

The OCR reads. The model understands. The gate decides. Only one of those three is allowed to be wrong quietly, and it is not the model.

The measurement that started everything

While I was still validating the OCR path, I rendered a test prescription in a handwriting font and read it back. Vision read it flawlessly and reported confidence 1.00 on every line.

One of the lines it read perfectly was this:

Ox: HTN, T2OM

That is Dx: HTN, T2DM with two letters misread. Nothing about that line was illegible. It was simply wrong, and the OCR was certain.

That taught me the number I had been planning to trust measures "were the pixels legible", not "is this thing real". So I threw it out as a safety signal and went looking for what could replace it.

Confidence scores being useless for this is not a new observation, and I did not discover it. sohakanu documented it precisely while building Scribe: median confidence 0.95 when right, 0.95 when wrong (Confidence Is Theater). Their fix was cross-model verification — reading each field twice with models that fail differently. raju_dandigam makes the same point from the other direction in A Confidence Score Is Not a Probability.

I took a different route, because a pharmacy has something a form does not: a fixed vocabulary. The shop knows which forty medicines it actually stocks. That is checkable in code, for free.

So I wrote 20 poisoned drug names

I built a test set of twenty lines, each a realistic OCR corruption of a real Indian brand: 0 misread as O, 1 as l, 5 as S.

Then I ran them through gemma3:4b and sorted every answer into one of four buckets:

bucket meaning
repaired returned the true medicine
refused declined to name one — safe
echoed_garbage accepted the corrupted string as a medicine — dangerous
silent_wrong invented a different medicine — dangerous

The last two are tracked together, because from the patient's side they are the same failure: a wrong medicine dispensed with confidence.

What the base model did

Nine of twenty lines came back wrong. All nine came back at 0.95 confidence.

Eighteen of twenty answers scored 0.90 or above. Nine of those eighteen were wrong. The confidence column carried no signal whatsoever, which means a threshold gate built on it would have passed nine wrong prescriptions straight through to the counter.

Two failure modes did the damage, and I only understood the second one by reading the eval output line by line.

It substituted generics for brands. Asked about Glycomet 6P2, it answered Metformin. For Pan 4O it answered Panadol. For Atorva 1O, Atorvastatin.

These are not cosmetic swaps. Glycomet GP2 contains glimepiride as well as metformin. Panadol is paracetamol; Pan is pantoprazole. A generic substitution is a different prescription.

And it is invisible in the JSON — except in one place. The name it returned is not anywhere on the page.

So I check exactly that. The longest word in the returned drug name gets compared against the raw OCR text with an OCR-sized edit tolerance:

def _grounding_problems(line: RxLine) -> list[str]:
    """Does the medicine the model named actually appear on the page?"""
    if not line.drug or not line.raw:
        return []

    drug_tokens = {t for t in tokens(normalise(line.drug)) if len(t) >= 3}
    if not drug_tokens:
        return []

    source_tokens = tokens(normalise(line.raw))
    anchor = max(drug_tokens, key=len)

    if any(closely_matches(anchor, source) for source in source_tokens):
        return []

    return [
        f"'{line.drug}' does not appear on the page as written "
        f"(OCR line reads: {line.raw.strip()!r})"
    ]

Checking that a value actually appears in its source is a known and documented technique — michael_maurice lays out the full discipline, including the crucial repairable/non-repairable split, in Schema-Valid Isn't Correct. I am applying it to brand names rather than invoice totals.

That one check caught all five substitutions the model made.

The second failure mode took me a whole eval run to see

With grounding in place, four of the nine were still getting through. All four were the same shape:

thyronorm-o-for-zero   strength='5Omcg'
ecosprin-s-for-five    strength='7S'
amlopres-s-for-five    strength='2.S'
insulin-units-word     strength='1O units'

Every one was the same thing. The drug name was correct, and it was genuinely on the page, so grounding had nothing to say about it. The strength was the corruption: 5O should be 50, 7S should be 75, 2.S should be 2.5, 1O units should be 10 units.

And my gate had accepted all four, because I was checking that the strength field was non-empty. Not that it was a strength.

Two regexes closed the gap. One for what a dose looks like, and one for the Indian combination markers that are legitimate strengths without being numbers at all:

_DOSE_RE   = re.compile(r"^\d+(?:\.\d+)?(?:mg|mcg|mgs|g|gm|ml|iu|units|unit|%)?$")
_SUFFIX_RE = re.compile(r"^[a-z]{1,3}\d+$")   # GP2 in Glycomet GP2

def _strength_problems(strength: str | None) -> list[str]:
    if not strength:
        return []

    compact = re.sub(r"\s+", "", strength)
    if _DOSE_RE.match(compact.lower()) or _SUFFIX_RE.match(compact.lower()):
        return []

    # If the digits are recoverable, say what we think it was. Suggesting a
    # correction is safe; applying one silently is not.
    guess = _repair_digits(compact)
    if guess != compact.lower() and _DOSE_RE.match(guess):
        return [
            f"strength {strength!r} does not parse as a strength "
            f"(looks like {guess!r} with a letter misread for a digit)"
        ]

    return [f"strength {strength!r} does not parse as a strength"]

Four misses went to zero. A wrong dose and a wrong drug are the same amount of wrong.

The false alarm I shipped, and how it surfaced

A word on false alarms, because a gate that cries wolf is a gate people click through. Three lines that the eval scores as safe still get sent to review: one where the model refused outright, one where it put x 30 days in the sig field, and the deliberately-illegible control case. I read all three. None is a correct answer being wrongly held back — they are the gate doing its job on a field my eval was not scoring.

Then, while reading the demo output above, I found one that was.

The strength check was flagging the GP2 in Glycomet GP2 as unparseable. GP2 is a combination marker — metformin plus glimepiride — and my regex only accepted digits with an optional unit. It was rejecting a correct answer, and no test caught it, because every test I had written encoded the same wrong assumption the code did. It surfaced because a human read the output.

That is now scripts/selfcheck.py: 53 checks covering the gate, the formulary, the counselling text and the end-to-end path, runnable with plain python3, no model and nothing to install. Two of those checks exist purely because of how the fix went wrong the first time — 1O units repaired to 10unit5 (the s in "units" was being read as a 5), and xyz acquired a confident repair hint for no reason at all. A wrong suggestion on a dosage is worse than no suggestion.

The same wrong assumption turned out to be sitting in the hosted demo's fixture too, a day later: the fixture had Glycomet GP2 with a null strength, so the gate reported "tablet with no strength" on a line whose strength was right there in the name. The real extractor returns GP2 in the strength field. The fixture was less realistic than the model it was standing in for, and it took reading the deployed page to notice.

Where it landed

base model with the shop's own correction history
wrong answers 9/20 (45%) 6/20 (30%)
correct 9/20 13/20
filled with no human looking 7/20 11/20
wrong answers reaching the counter 0/20 0/20

The model is still wrong a third of the time. None of it reaches the patient, because the gate does not accept the model's word for anything it can check itself.

The correction loop, and a result I did not expect

Every line the pharmacist corrects is written to a local SQLite table on the shop's machine. Those corrections are the shop's own vocabulary: in this shop, this handwriting, "Telrna" is Telma.

I fed 18 of them back into the prompt as context and re-ran the eval. It improved things: 45% wrong down to 30%, and four more lines filled without a human.

But it also introduced three regressions I would have missed if I had only looked at the totals:

glycomet-g-to-6     silent_wrong -> echoed_garbage   ("Glycomet 6P2" -> "Glycomet", GP2 dropped)
telmikind-h         repaired     -> echoed_garbage   ("Telmikind-H"  -> "Telmikind", -H dropped)
montck-dropped-e    silent_wrong -> echoed_garbage   ("Montck LC"    -> "Montck LC")

Given the shop's vocabulary, the model starts snapping to the nearest familiar name and silently drops suffixes that change what the medicine is. Telmikind-H contains a diuretic. Telmikind does not.

So the correction history is not a free win. It is a trade: better recovery of corrupted strengths, at the cost of a new way to be confidently wrong. The gate catches all three anyway, which is the point of having a gate that does not care how confident the model sounds.

This is also the honest reason the corrections matter. A hosted API cannot learn that this shop's handwriting turns Telma into Telrna, because the corrections are the most private thing in the building. They stay on the machine, and they are what a fine-tune would later be built from — via Tinker, so the shop never needs a GPU.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Three reasons, in the order they actually matter to the shopkeeper.

The data cannot leave. A prescription carries a patient's name, age, diagnosis and medicines. That is the most sensitive record the shop holds. The whole point is that the model runs where the data already is. Shipping it to a hosted database to prove the model is local would give away the thing being protected.

The vocabulary is local knowledge. Knowing that this shop stocks forty specific brands, and that in this handwriting Telrna means Telma, is not general knowledge. It is not in anyone's training data. It exists only in that shop, and it is the difference between a system that works and a system that is confidently wrong. Owning the model is what makes the correction loop worth building.

Volume makes per-call pricing cruel. This is not a chat app. It is a shop doing a couple of hundred pages a day, forever. A per-page API bill is a recurring cost that grows with the shop's success. A local model costs electricity and a laptop the shop already owns — and the slowest thing in the pipeline is the part I did not pay for.

There is a fourth reason I did not expect. Running locally meant I could measure the model's failures on the shop's real material, as many times as I wanted, for free. The 20-line eval that this whole post is about cost nothing to run eleven times. That is not really possible when every run is a billed API call.

And a fifth, which is the one this post is really about. Running locally meant I could read the raw output. The generic-for-brand substitution at 0.95 confidence is not visible in an aggregate score. Neither was the false alarm I had shipped in my own gate. Both were found by looking at what actually came back, one line at a time, on a machine I owned.

The hosted demo makes the same point from the other side. Every capability I had to switch off to make it fit on a free container — the model itself, the forecaster, the voice — is a capability that works when the software sits next to the data and the patient.

My Agent Session

The bug I am least proud of, and the one that taught me the most: the false positive above was invisible to every test I had, because I had written the tests from the same wrong assumption as the code. Here is the session where reading the real output caught it.

Finding a false positive in a prescription safety gate
You

Continue if you have next steps, or stop and ask for clarification if you are unsure how to proceed.

Agent

I'd just refactored the formulary to share a tolerant matcher between the food-timing table and the chronic list. My test only re-ran the cases I had changed, which passed. Let me re-run the whole thing instead, on every entry.

It immediately blew up. food_timing("Glycomet GP2") raised KeyError. The shared matcher normalises hyphens to spaces and returns that normalised key, but FOOD_TIMING was still keyed "glycomet-gp2" with a hyphen. So it matched, then failed to index the table. Every hyphenated entry was broken.

▸ bash .venv/bin/python -c "from app.formulary import food_timing; food_timing('Glyc...
Input
$ .venv/bin/python -c "from app.formulary import food_timing; food_timing('Glycomet GP2')"

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. The understanding layer is Google's gemma3:4b, served locally through Ollama, running on the CPU of an eight-core laptop with no GPU. It is the only reason the "generic becomes brand" substitution is visible at all: the model reads Glycomet 6P2 and reaches for the only metformin brand it has ever heard of. Every safety check in the system exists because Gemma is useful and unreliable in a specific, measurable way — and because it runs locally, I could measure exactly how unreliable, eleven times over, for nothing.

Best Use of TabPFN. The shop's second problem is knowing what to reorder, and it is a tabular forecasting problem of exactly the kind a chemist cannot answer from memory: a dozen medicines, three months of dispense counts, and spiky demand around festivals. app/tabpfn_engine.py builds a weekly series per medicine and fits Prior Labs' TabPFN walk-forward — never training on a week it is about to predict — then ranks by urgency, weighted for the chronic medicines that must never run out.

It forecasts demand per medicine, not refills per patient. That is deliberate: the dispenses table has no patient column, because it is the only table that could leave the machine without carrying anyone's medical history with it. The richer signal would have cost the privacy claim the whole project rests on.

One detail I would keep in any system like this: without requirements-ml.txt the forecaster silently falls back to a damped moving average, so every row carries the method that produced it — "method": "tabpfn (53 shop rows)". A fallback can never be mistaken for a forecast. That field is also how I discovered that tabpfn was not installed at all while the code claimed it was, which is a lesson about the difference between integrating a library and running one.

Best Use of ElevenLabs. The last mile of a prescription is the part the pharmacist has already said fifty times before lunch: what to take, when to take it, for how long, and what to do if something goes wrong. That explanation is spoken, not read. Many of the people this shop serves would rather hear it than read a label, and by the fiftieth time the pharmacist is no longer saying all of it.

ElevenLabs' eleven_multilingual_v2 renders that script in Hindi from prompts/counsel.txt, and the parts he drops are exactly the parts written into the prompt: never take two doses at once to catch up on a missed one, come back to the shop with the strip if anything is unclear, and see a doctor immediately for a rash, swelling or difficulty breathing. It is a real render — 485 characters in, 39 seconds of Hindi out, at one credit per character — and it is checked into the repo as demo/counselling-hindi.mp3 so it can be listened to rather than taken on trust.

One thing I got wrong first and would have shipped: I originally rendered it with a default English premade voice. eleven_multilingual_v2 will happily make an American voice read Devanagari script, and it sounds exactly as wrong as that suggests — a patient being told their dosage in a foreign accent. Auditioning the Hindi voices in the shared library and switching to a native one cost 240 credits and one afternoon. Worth saying out loud, because "the multilingual model speaks Hindi" and "the voice sounds like it speaks Hindi" are two different claims, and only the first one is the model's job.

The design decision I would defend is that the audio is opt-in per request and off by default. It is the only step in the pipeline that sends anything off the machine, and what it sends necessarily contains the medicine names — a patient cannot be told to take something the sentence refuses to name. So the text stays local and the pharmacist asks for the speech. The hosted demo has no key at all, for the same reason.

Best Use of Render. The hosted demo above is deployed from a Render blueprint — render.yaml lives in the repository, so the service is described in version control rather than clicked together in a dashboard, and a stranger can reproduce the deploy from the repo alone.

The interesting part was making a free-tier container honest. There is no GPU and 512MB of RAM, so instead of pretending, the deployment was designed around the constraint: requirements.txt and requirements-ml.txt are separate files so the deployable dependency set stays small enough to build without dragging in torch, app/main.py never imports the macOS Vision wrapper (app/ocr.py) so the Linux container boots, and DEMO_MODE=true replays the real recorded OCR transcript while the gate, the forecaster and the counselling text all execute for real. The page tells you which parts are fixtures and why, which is the only reason I would put a demo link in a post about not trusting things.

Thanks to sohakanu, michael_maurice, raju_dandigam and hexisteme — this project would have taken a much longer route to a worse place without their write-ups.

All names, prescriptions and corrections in this post are synthetic. No real patient data was used, and no page left the machine.

event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

A prescription reader for a neighbourhood medical shop in India. It runs on the shop's own laptop, with no network connection at all.

The shopkeeper photographs a handwritten prescription. The system reads it, works out what was actually prescribed, and decides for itself which lines are safe to fill and which ones need a human to look at the paper.

The person who would pay for this is the chemist himself. He currently re-reads every prescription by hand because he cannot afford to get one wrong, and he is doing it at 9pm after a fourteen-hour day.

I should be upfront that the interesting part of this project is not the reading. It is the deciding when not to trust the reading.

Demo

The whole pipeline runs from one command on the shop's machine:

python3 scripts/run_page.py prescription.jpg

A synthetic page, end to end:

--- OCR (1.77s wall, 1.64s engine, 11 observations -> 9 lines) ---
  [conf 1.00] Dr. R.Deshmukh MBBSReg2019/4482
  [conf 1.00] Pt: Mr. Suresh Wankhede 42/M
  [conf 1.00] Ox: HTN, T2OM
  [conf 1.00] Rx
  [conf 1.00] 1. Tab Telma 40mg 1-0-0 x 30 days
  [conf 1.00] 2. Tab Glycomet GP2 1-0-1 x 30 days
  [conf 1.00] 3. Cap Pan 40 1-0-0 x15 days
  [conf 1.00] 4. Inj. Insulin 0-0-1 x 10 days
  [conf 1.00] Adv: review after 15 days

--- reconciled prescription (57.1s wall) ---
  diagnosis: HTN, T2DM
  [0] Telma 40mg Tab sig=1-0-0 days=30 conf=0.70
  [1] Glycomet GP2 Tab sig=1-0-1 days=30 conf=0.70
  [2] Pan 40 Cap sig=1-0-0 days=15 conf=0.60
  [3] Insulin Inj sig=0-0-1 days=10 conf=0.60

--- gate: review ---
  - line 1 (Telma): model confidence 0.70 is below 0.80
  - line 2 (Glycomet): model confidence 0.70 is below 0.80
  - line 3 (Pan): model confidence 0.60 is below 0.80
  - line 4 (Insulin): model confidence 0.60 is below 0.80

total: 58.9s (OCR 1.8s + model 57.1s)

Look at the third OCR line and then the diagnosis line underneath it. Those are the same characters read two different ways: the OCR returned Ox: HTN, T2OM, and the model worked out that it was Dx: HTN, T2DM. That is the one thing here the model does genuinely better than any regex I could write.

The other thing worth noticing is that on this page, every line goes to a human. That is entirely the confidence threshold, not the interesting checks, because the model was candid enough to score its own repairs at 0.60–0.70. The structural checks are what earn their place on the poisoned set further down, where the model is not candid and hands back 0.95 on answers that are wrong.

On the timing: 57s is the steady state. The first page after the model has been idle takes about 80s, because gemma3:4b has to be loaded into memory first. I have not tried to hide that number. On an eight-core laptop with no GPU it is the real price of not sending the page anywhere.

A hosted copy, and a precise list of what it does not do

parchi-hub8.onrender.com

I want to be exact about the limits of that link, because the limits happen to be the argument.

It replays the real recorded OCR transcript from the page above — not a mock-up of one, the actual Vision output, including the Ox: HTN, T2OM line. The gate, the reorder forecast and the Hindi counselling text all execute live against it. If you want to see the gate refuse something, it is the line 3 (Pan) entry in the "Why" column.

What it does not do is run gemma3:4b. Render's free tier is a Linux container with 512MB of RAM and no GPU, and the model is 3.4GB. So the reading step is a deterministic fixture, and the page says so on itself rather than pretending.

Two consequences, stated rather than left for you to find:

  • The forecast on that instance reports "method": "damped-mean", not TabPFN. Torch does not fit there either; requirements-ml.txt is what switches TabPFN on, and the fallback announces itself in that field — which is the whole reason the field exists.
  • There is no audio on that instance, deliberately. The speech works: demo/counselling-hindi.mp3 in the repo is a real render, 39 seconds of Hindi, checked in so you can listen without a key. But the key is not set on a public host, because an open endpoint that spends credits on every request is a bill that anyone who finds the URL can run up. The key stays on the shop's machine.

That last point is the project's own thesis turned back on itself, so it seemed like the wrong thing to make an exception for.

Code

github.com/kotewar/parchi

The pieces worth reading:

  • app/gate.py — the deterministic safety checks, including the two that mattered most
  • app/gemma.py — the local model call, with the two API gotchas commented so nobody re-breaks them
  • app/tabpfn_engine.py — refill forecasting from the shop's own dispense history
  • scripts/selfcheck.py — 53 regression checks, runnable with plain python3, no model, no setup
  • scripts/eval.py — the poisoned-name eval harness
  • data/eval_poisoned.json — the 20 test lines and their ground truth
  • eval_base_v2.json and eval_primed_v2.json — the two runs quoted below, committed so the claims are checkable

How I Built It

I started by trying to get a vision model to read the handwriting. That was the wrong instinct, and the community had already measured why: a dedicated OCR engine is roughly 300x faster than a general-purpose vision model at reading, with fewer character errors (The Dedicated OCR Engine Lost to the General Purpose Model by hexisteme).

So the architecture splits the job:

page image
   -> macOS Vision OCR        (reading: 1.8s/page)
   -> gemma3:4b via Ollama    (meaning: what is this medicine?)
   -> deterministic gate      (safety: may this be filled?)
   -> human review            (only what the gate refuses)

The OCR reads. The model understands. The gate decides. Only one of those three is allowed to be wrong quietly, and it is not the model.

The measurement that started everything

While I was still validating the OCR path, I rendered a test prescription in a handwriting font and read it back. Vision read it flawlessly and reported confidence 1.00 on every line.

One of the lines it read perfectly was this:

Ox: HTN, T2OM

That is Dx: HTN, T2DM with two letters misread. Nothing about that line was illegible. It was simply wrong, and the OCR was certain.

That taught me the number I had been planning to trust measures "were the pixels legible", not "is this thing real". So I threw it out as a safety signal and went looking for what could replace it.

Confidence scores being useless for this is not a new observation, and I did not discover it. sohakanu documented it precisely while building Scribe: median confidence 0.95 when right, 0.95 when wrong (Confidence Is Theater). Their fix was cross-model verification — reading each field twice with models that fail differently. raju_dandigam makes the same point from the other direction in A Confidence Score Is Not a Probability.

I took a different route, because a pharmacy has something a form does not: a fixed vocabulary. The shop knows which forty medicines it actually stocks. That is checkable in code, for free.

So I wrote 20 poisoned drug names

I built a test set of twenty lines, each a realistic OCR corruption of a real Indian brand: 0 misread as O, 1 as l, 5 as S.

Then I ran them through gemma3:4b and sorted every answer into one of four buckets:

bucket meaning
repaired returned the true medicine
refused declined to name one — safe
echoed_garbage accepted the corrupted string as a medicine — dangerous
silent_wrong invented a different medicine — dangerous

The last two are tracked together, because from the patient's side they are the same failure: a wrong medicine dispensed with confidence.

What the base model did

Nine of twenty lines came back wrong. All nine came back at 0.95 confidence.

Eighteen of twenty answers scored 0.90 or above. Nine of those eighteen were wrong. The confidence column carried no signal whatsoever, which means a threshold gate built on it would have passed nine wrong prescriptions straight through to the counter.

Two failure modes did the damage, and I only understood the second one by reading the eval output line by line.

It substituted generics for brands. Asked about Glycomet 6P2, it answered Metformin. For Pan 4O it answered Panadol. For Atorva 1O, Atorvastatin.

These are not cosmetic swaps. Glycomet GP2 contains glimepiride as well as metformin. Panadol is paracetamol; Pan is pantoprazole. A generic substitution is a different prescription.

And it is invisible in the JSON — except in one place. The name it returned is not anywhere on the page.

So I check exactly that. The longest word in the returned drug name gets compared against the raw OCR text with an OCR-sized edit tolerance:

def _grounding_problems(line: RxLine) -> list[str]:
    """Does the medicine the model named actually appear on the page?"""
    if not line.drug or not line.raw:
        return []

    drug_tokens = {t for t in tokens(normalise(line.drug)) if len(t) >= 3}
    if not drug_tokens:
        return []

    source_tokens = tokens(normalise(line.raw))
    anchor = max(drug_tokens, key=len)

    if any(closely_matches(anchor, source) for source in source_tokens):
        return []

    return [
        f"'{line.drug}' does not appear on the page as written "
        f"(OCR line reads: {line.raw.strip()!r})"
    ]

Checking that a value actually appears in its source is a known and documented technique — michael_maurice lays out the full discipline, including the crucial repairable/non-repairable split, in Schema-Valid Isn't Correct. I am applying it to brand names rather than invoice totals.

That one check caught all five substitutions the model made.

The second failure mode took me a whole eval run to see

With grounding in place, four of the nine were still getting through. All four were the same shape:

thyronorm-o-for-zero   strength='5Omcg'
ecosprin-s-for-five    strength='7S'
amlopres-s-for-five    strength='2.S'
insulin-units-word     strength='1O units'

Every one was the same thing. The drug name was correct, and it was genuinely on the page, so grounding had nothing to say about it. The strength was the corruption: 5O should be 50, 7S should be 75, 2.S should be 2.5, 1O units should be 10 units.

And my gate had accepted all four, because I was checking that the strength field was non-empty. Not that it was a strength.

Two regexes closed the gap. One for what a dose looks like, and one for the Indian combination markers that are legitimate strengths without being numbers at all:

_DOSE_RE   = re.compile(r"^\d+(?:\.\d+)?(?:mg|mcg|mgs|g|gm|ml|iu|units|unit|%)?$")
_SUFFIX_RE = re.compile(r"^[a-z]{1,3}\d+$")   # GP2 in Glycomet GP2

def _strength_problems(strength: str | None) -> list[str]:
    if not strength:
        return []

    compact = re.sub(r"\s+", "", strength)
    if _DOSE_RE.match(compact.lower()) or _SUFFIX_RE.match(compact.lower()):
        return []

    # If the digits are recoverable, say what we think it was. Suggesting a
    # correction is safe; applying one silently is not.
    guess = _repair_digits(compact)
    if guess != compact.lower() and _DOSE_RE.match(guess):
        return [
            f"strength {strength!r} does not parse as a strength "
            f"(looks like {guess!r} with a letter misread for a digit)"
        ]

    return [f"strength {strength!r} does not parse as a strength"]

Four misses went to zero. A wrong dose and a wrong drug are the same amount of wrong.

The false alarm I shipped, and how it surfaced

A word on false alarms, because a gate that cries wolf is a gate people click through. Three lines that the eval scores as safe still get sent to review: one where the model refused outright, one where it put x 30 days in the sig field, and the deliberately-illegible control case. I read all three. None is a correct answer being wrongly held back — they are the gate doing its job on a field my eval was not scoring.

Then, while reading the demo output above, I found one that was.

The strength check was flagging the GP2 in Glycomet GP2 as unparseable. GP2 is a combination marker — metformin plus glimepiride — and my regex only accepted digits with an optional unit. It was rejecting a correct answer, and no test caught it, because every test I had written encoded the same wrong assumption the code did. It surfaced because a human read the output.

That is now scripts/selfcheck.py: 53 checks covering the gate, the formulary, the counselling text and the end-to-end path, runnable with plain python3, no model and nothing to install. Two of those checks exist purely because of how the fix went wrong the first time — 1O units repaired to 10unit5 (the s in "units" was being read as a 5), and xyz acquired a confident repair hint for no reason at all. A wrong suggestion on a dosage is worse than no suggestion.

The same wrong assumption turned out to be sitting in the hosted demo's fixture too, a day later: the fixture had Glycomet GP2 with a null strength, so the gate reported "tablet with no strength" on a line whose strength was right there in the name. The real extractor returns GP2 in the strength field. The fixture was less realistic than the model it was standing in for, and it took reading the deployed page to notice.

Where it landed

base model with the shop's own correction history
wrong answers 9/20 (45%) 6/20 (30%)
correct 9/20 13/20
filled with no human looking 7/20 11/20
wrong answers reaching the counter 0/20 0/20

The model is still wrong a third of the time. None of it reaches the patient, because the gate does not accept the model's word for anything it can check itself.

The correction loop, and a result I did not expect

Every line the pharmacist corrects is written to a local SQLite table on the shop's machine. Those corrections are the shop's own vocabulary: in this shop, this handwriting, "Telrna" is Telma.

I fed 18 of them back into the prompt as context and re-ran the eval. It improved things: 45% wrong down to 30%, and four more lines filled without a human.

But it also introduced three regressions I would have missed if I had only looked at the totals:

glycomet-g-to-6     silent_wrong -> echoed_garbage   ("Glycomet 6P2" -> "Glycomet", GP2 dropped)
telmikind-h         repaired     -> echoed_garbage   ("Telmikind-H"  -> "Telmikind", -H dropped)
montck-dropped-e    silent_wrong -> echoed_garbage   ("Montck LC"    -> "Montck LC")

Given the shop's vocabulary, the model starts snapping to the nearest familiar name and silently drops suffixes that change what the medicine is. Telmikind-H contains a diuretic. Telmikind does not.

So the correction history is not a free win. It is a trade: better recovery of corrupted strengths, at the cost of a new way to be confidently wrong. The gate catches all three anyway, which is the point of having a gate that does not care how confident the model sounds.

This is also the honest reason the corrections matter. A hosted API cannot learn that this shop's handwriting turns Telma into Telrna, because the corrections are the most private thing in the building. They stay on the machine, and they are what a fine-tune would later be built from — via Tinker, so the shop never needs a GPU.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Three reasons, in the order they actually matter to the shopkeeper.

The data cannot leave. A prescription carries a patient's name, age, diagnosis and medicines. That is the most sensitive record the shop holds. The whole point is that the model runs where the data already is. Shipping it to a hosted database to prove the model is local would give away the thing being protected.

The vocabulary is local knowledge. Knowing that this shop stocks forty specific brands, and that in this handwriting Telrna means Telma, is not general knowledge. It is not in anyone's training data. It exists only in that shop, and it is the difference between a system that works and a system that is confidently wrong. Owning the model is what makes the correction loop worth building.

Volume makes per-call pricing cruel. This is not a chat app. It is a shop doing a couple of hundred pages a day, forever. A per-page API bill is a recurring cost that grows with the shop's success. A local model costs electricity and a laptop the shop already owns — and the slowest thing in the pipeline is the part I did not pay for.

There is a fourth reason I did not expect. Running locally meant I could measure the model's failures on the shop's real material, as many times as I wanted, for free. The 20-line eval that this whole post is about cost nothing to run eleven times. That is not really possible when every run is a billed API call.

And a fifth, which is the one this post is really about. Running locally meant I could read the raw output. The generic-for-brand substitution at 0.95 confidence is not visible in an aggregate score. Neither was the false alarm I had shipped in my own gate. Both were found by looking at what actually came back, one line at a time, on a machine I owned.

The hosted demo makes the same point from the other side. Every capability I had to switch off to make it fit on a free container — the model itself, the forecaster, the voice — is a capability that works when the software sits next to the data and the patient.

My Agent Session

The bug I am least proud of, and the one that taught me the most: the false positive above was invisible to every test I had, because I had written the tests from the same wrong assumption as the code. Here is the session where reading the real output caught it.

Prize Categories

Best Use of TabPFN. The shop's second problem is knowing what to reorder, and it is a tabular forecasting problem of exactly the kind a chemist cannot answer from memory: a dozen medicines, three months of dispense counts, and spiky demand around festivals. app/tabpfn_engine.py builds a weekly series per medicine and fits Prior Labs' TabPFN walk-forward — never training on a week it is about to predict — then ranks by urgency, weighted for the chronic medicines that must never run out.

Auditioning the Hindi voices in the shared library and switching to a native one cost 240 credits and one afternoon. The design decision I would defend is that the audio is opt-in per request and off by default. It is the only step in the pipeline that sends anything off the machine, and what it sends necessarily contains the medicine names — a patient cannot be told to take something the sentence refuses to name. So the text stays local and the pharmacist asks for the speech. The hosted demo has no key at all, for the same reason.

Best Use of Render. The hosted demo above is deployed from a Render blueprint — render.yaml lives in the repository, so the service is described in version control rather than clicked together in a dashboard, and a stranger can reproduce the deploy from the repo alone.

The interesting part was making a free-tier container honest. There is no GPU and 512MB of RAM, so instead of pretending, the deployment was designed around the constraint: requirements.txt and requirements-ml.txt are separate files so the deployable dependency set stays small enough to build without dragging in torch, app/main.py never imports the macOS Vision wrapper (app/ocr.py) so the Linux container boots, and DEMO_MODE=true replays the real recorded OCR transcript while the gate, the forecaster and the counselling text all execute for real. The page tells you which parts are fixtures and why, which is the only reason I would put a demo link in a post about not trusting things.

Thanks to sohakanu, michael_maurice, raju_dandigam and hexisteme — this project would have taken a much longer route to a worse place without their write-ups.

All names, prescriptions and corrections in this post are synthetic. No real patient data was used, and no page left the machine.

title: My read-only Python scanner accidentally ran a Git helper
summary:
We were building a tool whose defining promise was simple: inspect unfamiliar repository configuration without executing its code. Then a test revealed that an ordinary-looking Git operation could launch a program defined by the repository itself.

A small assumption with big consequences

You're about to open a GitHub repository in your editor. You want to know which commands may run through package installation, trusted workspace tasks, devcontainer startup, MCP servers or an AI coding agent. A static auditor looks like a reasonable first line of review.

ClonePeek was designed for that job. Its scanner traverses recognized configuration files using bounded reads and reports trigger → command → source location → suggested review , without launching the project's npm scripts, shell hooks, or coding agents.

There is a useful optional flag: --changed-since filters findings to Git changes. Our first implementation called a local git diff command. It felt harmless. Diffing files isn't building the repository, right?

The catch is that Git's execution behavior can depend on checkout-local or inherited configuration, not just the arguments my code passes. In particular, a local core.fsmonitor setting can name a hook-like helper program. Depending on the command and Git version, Git may invoke that helper while refreshing file state. A subprocess invoked by the auditor was therefore enough to break our passive-scan invariant.

One important boundary: a normal git clone does not transfer the remote repo's .git/config. The issue is an existing checkout and its local configuration or inherited Git environment; don't confuse it with a malicious package.json remotely rewriting Git config simply by being cloned.

Making the regression observable

To test this safely, we created a disposable local fixture with a deliberately inert helper that merely wrote a marker file. We did not use a real suspicious repository, download an executable payload, or depend on a network request.

The test asked one specific question: can the audit complete without creating that marker? Before the fix, the marker appeared. After the fix, it did not. Reproducing the violation as a filesystem side effect made it much harder for later refactors to accidentally reintroduce it.

This is not a claim that every git diff invocation on every operating system will execute an fsmonitor helper. It's a concrete example of why "I only ran Git" doesn't establish that no repo-defined execution occurred.

The exact reproduction and safety constraints are in the Git configuration isolation notes; the patch and review trail are in PR #5.

The defense has to cover the helper process

Python's read-only filesystem operations were not the issue. The boundary changed when the scanner delegated work to Git, a separate executable capable of honoring configuration, helpers and extensions. Fixing it required controlling both process arguments and the environment.

# Excerpted structure, not a standalone security sandbox
argv = [
    "git",
    "-c", "core.fsmonitor=false",
    "-c", f"core.hooksPath={os.devnull}",
    "-c", "diff.external=",
    "-c", "protocol.ext.allow=never",
    "-c", "protocol.file.allow=never",
    "-C", str(repo_root),
    "diff", "--no-ext-diff", "--no-textconv",
    "--name-only", "-z", "--diff-filter=ACMR",
    reference, "--",
]

The scanner also strips inherited Git-specific variables and dangerous loader/Python environment overrides, disables system/global Git config for this invocation, rejects unexpected ref syntax, bounds subprocess runtime, and treats a failed diff as an error rather than silently reporting an empty result. These are defense-in-depth choices for an explicitly limited operation ; they are not equivalent to process isolation.

Important limit: This hardening is targeted to the Git invocation used by ClonePeek. Git and the host operating system have more behavior than one wrapper can model. Do not treat ClonePeek as a sandbox, a malware detector, or a reliable way to execute other tools against actively malicious content.

The next surprise was a script one file away

Another coverage gap turned out to be less dramatic but equally useful. A package.json file could contain a short lifecycle command such as sh ./scripts/setup.sh. A surface-only scanner recognized the install hook, but the interesting command might live inside scripts/setup.sh, outside the JSON.

We added bounded, first-hop, read-only inspection for statically identifiable local .sh references. It checks that paths stay inside the repository, rejects symlink escapes and unsafe file types, and limits references, file sizes and lines read. It doesn't shell-expand arbitrary expressions or chase unbounded nested scripts.

That sounds modest—and that's intentional. A scanner that executes the referenced script "to find out what it does" would solve one detection problem by discarding its own execution boundary. ClonePeek instead tells you what it can and can't see.

Testing a release from outside the repository

Internal tests can miss assumptions about packaging. The v0.5.0 GitHub Action therefore has separate integration CI on Linux, macOS and Windows, plus an actual consumer workflow in another repository. That consumer workflow read two pinned, public configuration snapshots (Cursor hooks and VS Code folder-open tasks), checked their Git blob hashes, and asserted paths and classifications. No upstream hooks were run.

These are narrow smoke tests, not independent outside-user adoption or an estimate of detection accuracy. The hand-authored synthetic evaluation deliberately includes false positives and false negatives; it is not representative of internet repositories.

A checklist for tools that inspect untrusted projects

  • Map all execution paths, including your own helper commands. A safe-looking wrapper doesn't make delegated subprocesses inert.
  • Write regression tests around side effects, not only output strings. A marker file can reveal unexpected execution even when the scanner report looks correct.
  • Constrain filesystem reads and traversal. Symlinks, special files, large files and path escapes matter even when you never execute a script.
  • Separate supported detection from safety claims. A command hook is a review prompt, not proof that an author is malicious.
  • Make failure visible. Parse errors and unsupported references should not silently become "nothing found."

If you're auditing a repository you don't trust, the safest workflow begins before installing its dependencies or marking it trusted in an IDE. The five-minute pre-trust audit guide covers practical next steps.

Try it. Critique it. Improve it.

ClonePeek v0.5.1 is MIT licensed, has no runtime Python dependencies, and exposes its threat model publicly. We're looking for real, inert examples of execution hooks it misses or overclassifies—not drive-by stars or artificial PRs.

uvx --from git+https://github.com/harshitethic/clonepeek@v0.5.1 \
  clonepeek /path/to/repository

Browse source ↗ Contribute a real improvement ↗ Live demo ↗

Disclosure: I maintain ClonePeek. This case study was prepared with AI writing assistance and reviewed against the source, tests, and public docs. Maintainer-run tests are not independent security evaluation.
