title: PostgreSQL 19 Slips to November as AI Code Review Finds Bugs Faster Than Humans Can Fix Them
summary:
PostgreSQL 19 Slips to November as AI Code Review Finds Bugs Faster Than Humans Can Fix Them

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group has delayed PostgreSQL 19, pushing general availability from the original late-September/early-October target to around November 19, 2026 — and the culprit, remarkably, is not sloppy engineering. It is the opposite: AI-assisted code review has become so effective that it is finding problems faster than the volunteer-driven project can fix them.

According to a detailed account from leading PostgreSQL committer Peter Eisentraut, VP at support and consultancy firm EDB, the release team has reverted somewhere between eight and ten significant features from PostgreSQL 19, deferring them to PostgreSQL 20. While some of those reverts stem from genuine architectural defects that could not be patched "quickly and during beta," Eisentraut attributes a substantial share of the disruption to something new: LLM-assisted code review raising the project's effective quality standards mid-cycle, on patches that were written before the tooling became powerful enough to catch their flaws.

A list of forty defect reports nobody had time for

The mechanics of the delay are almost mundane. During the extended beta window, LLM-assisted review surfaced roughly forty defect reports — a long tail of "relatively harmless issues involving various edge cases" that in previous release cycles would likely have trickled out as post-release bug fixes over the following five years. As Eisentraut put it: "With LLM-assisted code review, these kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you're staring at a list of forty defect reports."

Every one of those reports still needs a human committer to read it, confirm it is real, write a fix, test it, and get it reviewed under PostgreSQL's commit policies. "Even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time," Eisentraut explained. Forty tickets at even modest triage cost per item adds up to days or weeks of committer attention that a project operating on an annual release clock simply did not have before the planned freeze.

The result is an unusual situation for one of the world's most widely deployed open source databases: a release that is late not because the tooling failed, but because it worked.

SQL/PGQ and the biggest casualties

The highest-profile feature pulled from PostgreSQL 19 is support for SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ), the SQL-standard syntax added in 2023 for querying graph-style relationships between nodes and edges over relational data. Its implementation was removed over unresolved issues, after veteran contributor Tom Lane warned: "At this point I'd be willing to bet dinner that if we ship it in v19 there will be post-release bug discoveries that are unfixable until v20."

Eisentraut was careful to head off the obvious hot take. The reverts, he stressed, are not the result of "vibe coding" — AI-generated patches — because those techniques were not available when most of the affected features were originally written. The affected code predates the current wave of AI review tooling; what changed is the scrutiny applied to it after the fact.

What still ships

Despite the cuts, PostgreSQL 19 is still expected to be what Eisentraut calls "a great release." The headline survivor is REPACK CONCURRENTLY, which reclaims disk space without the heavy table locking that VACUUM FULL requires — a long-requested win for large production deployments. The project shipped Release Candidate 1 on October 15, with a second release candidate scheduled for November 12 ahead of the November 19 GA date.

There is a knock-on effect for PostgreSQL 20, too. Just a few months ago, developers expected PG 20 to be a quiet, bug-fix-oriented release. Now it is likely to absorb the reverted features from PG 19, making it unusually feature-rich.

Why this matters beyond Postgres

The PostgreSQL episode is worth watching even if you never run the database, because it is a preview of a problem every serious software project is about to face. AI reviewers do not just accelerate finding bugs — they accelerate the accumulation of work. When a tool can surface in an afternoon the edge cases that would previously have taken five years of production incidents to discover, the bottleneck shifts decisively from detection to remediation.

For enterprises, the practical guidance is straightforward. Teams that budgeted Q4 2026 migration windows around the original October target now have a tighter runway into the November-December change freeze. Managed PostgreSQL providers will push their rollout timelines back accordingly. And those waiting specifically for SQL/PGQ graph queries will need to wait for PostgreSQL 20.

There is also a security dimension to this trend. PostgreSQL historically averaged a couple of CVEs per release cycle; the August 2026 patch release for PostgreSQL 18 shipped fixes for 28. The same AI-assisted tooling that is disrupting release schedules is also dramatically expanding the number of known vulnerabilities being found and fixed — a net positive, even if it makes release calendars messier.

The irony is hard to miss: PostgreSQL 19 will ship later than planned, but precisely because of that, it will likely arrive as a cleaner, better-audited baseline than the version that would have gone out on the original schedule. In an industry still arguing about whether AI makes software better or worse, Postgres just offered a data point on the uncomfortable middle: AI makes software better, but slower — at least until the humans catch up.

title: 'RCTBridge.h' file not found: I compiled every React Native 0.87 header to see which imports break
summary:
After upgrading to React Native 0.87 (or Expo SDK 58), some iOS builds stop inside a library:

node_modules/react-native-date-picker/ios/DatePicker.m:7:9: error: 'RCTComponent.h' file not found
node_modules/@react-native-menu/menu/ios/MenuViewManager.mm:3:9: 'RCTBridge.h' file not found

The release notes explain why in one line: React Native 0.87 ships its iOS headers as header-only XCFrameworks, and "if you import a React Native header without its namespace, add it". So #import becomes #import .

That leaves questions the notes don't answer. Does the quoted form #import "RCTBridge.h" break too? Every header, or some? What about apps that build React Native from source? I wanted NativeKeel to warn about this before an upgrade, so I needed exact answers, not a regex that cries wolf.

The experiment

I created a React Native 0.87.1 app (Xcode 26.2) and generated one source file per header: all 227 RCT*.h headers under react-native/React, each imported on its own, once as "RCTX.h" and once as . Then I compiled them twice: with the default prebuilt React Native core, and with RCT_USE_PREBUILT_RNCORE=0 (built from source).

Import Default (prebuilt) Built from source
#import works works
#import "RCTBridge.h" file not found works
#import file not found file not found

The exceptions are small but matter: in quotes, RCTFabricComponentsPlugins.h, RCTComponentViewHelpers.h, the CoreModules headers and RCTLocalizedString.h still resolve. That's why most Fabric libraries, which write #import "RCTFabricComponentsPlugins.h", build fine.

One more pattern is safe: an import inside an #if __has_include() … #else #import "RCTBridge.h" fallback. The compiler takes the first branch, and many older libraries are written exactly like that.

Which libraries hit it

With those rules, I scanned the iOS sources of the 248 most downloaded React Native libraries with native iOS code (16 October 2026). Five fail:

Library Import Status
react-native-date-picker 5.0.13 "RCTComponent.h", "RCTConvert.h" issue open
@react-native-menu/menu 2.0.0 "RCTBridge.h" fix proposed in a PR
react-native-bottom-tabs 1.4.0 "RCTConversions.h" fixed on main, next release
react-native-ios-context-menu 3.2.1 "RCTBridge.h" fix proposed in a PR
react-native-ios-utilities 5.2.0 "RCTBridge.h" no report yet

Three of them already have "file not found" reports from people who upgraded, which is a good sign the rules match reality. In the 1,040 open-source apps I test with, 31 depend on at least one of these five.

What to do

  1. Update the library if a release has the change.
  2. Otherwise patch the import and keep it with patch-package: 
   - #import "RCTComponent.h"
   + #import
  1. Temporary workaround: build React Native from source, where the quoted form still resolves: RCT_USE_PREBUILT_RNCORE=0 bundle exec pod install, or buildReactNativeFromSource: true under ios in expo-build-properties. Clean builds get much slower, and it doesn't help with .

Check your own AppDelegate and native modules too: the same rule applies to app code.

Finding it before the upgrade

NativeKeel now reads the iOS code of your installed libraries and your own ios/ folder. On React Native below 0.87 it lists these imports as work for the upgrade; on 0.87 and later it reports them as the reason the build fails, with file and line:

npx nativekeel

The full table, with links to each issue and PR: nativekeel.com/fix/rctcomponent-h-file-not-found-react-native-0-87.

If a library you use fails this way and isn't in the table, tell me and I'll add it.

title: Google Just Open-Sourced ML Drift, the GPU Engine Behind LiteRT. Here's What Changes for You
summary:
If you've ever tried to ship an ML model that runs fast on users' GPUs, you know the problem: you have no idea which GPU, driver or graphics API your app will meet. A Pixel, an iPhone, a browser tab and a Windows laptop all speak different dialects.

On 8 October, Google's AI Edge team open-sourced the engine it uses to deal with exactly that. It's called ML Drift, and if you use TensorFlow Lite or LiteRT, it affects you.

What ML Drift is

ML Drift is an open-source (Apache 2.0), cross-platform GPU compute engine built for on-device AI/ML inference. It hides the hardware and low-level API differences across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal and WebGPU.

It's the core GPU acceleration engine inside LiteRT (Google's on-device runtime), and it's also available as a standalone library if you're building your own graphics or inference runtime.

It isn't a research toy. Google says it already runs in production on millions of devices daily, in Chrome, YouTube Shorts, Photos and Meet.

Why it matters

One shader codebase instead of three. The old TFLite GPU delegate needed separately maintained shaders for OpenGL, OpenCL and Metal, with tensors hardcoded to physical GPU objects like textures and buffers. ML Drift introduces tensor virtualization: a tensor's logical layout is separated from how it's physically stored on the GPU, so one set of shader templates works across backends, with minimal runtime overhead according to Google.

5D tensors, finally. The legacy delegate was hardcoded to 4D tensors. ML Drift supports 5D out of the box, which helps 3D convolutional and spatiotemporal models. Google names YOLO 11n, MobileViT v2 and Swin Transformer v2 as examples.

Built with on-device LLMs in mind. LLM inference has a compute-heavy prefill stage and a memory-bandwidth-heavy decode stage. ML Drift switches kernels and layouts depending on which stage it's in. In Google's Gemma benchmarks, it used up to 12% less memory than other frameworks.

Desktop, too (in preview). The WebGPU backend, compiled natively through Dawn (Chromium's WebGPU implementation), lets ML Drift run on Windows and Linux, alongside a native Metal backend on macOS. Mobile and edge remain the main focus.

Custom ops are easier. There's a custom op framework with direct registration APIs, plus a SKILL.md guide that helps coding agents write, register and check custom shaders.

The production numbers Google shares: up to 40% lower average frame latency for YouTube Shorts effects on Android and iOS, up to 30% faster on-device performance for some Adobe Lightroom and Photoshop features, and 30% lower model latency for some Snapchat lens effects.

If you use the TFLite GPU delegate

This is the part to act on. The legacy TFLite GPU delegate will no longer receive new feature updates. Google recommends moving to the LiteRT ML Drift GPU accelerator, which it says is fully backwards compatible with existing models. Google also says models already running on TFLite GPU should maintain or beat their previous benchmarks.

One caveat for Android developers using unbundled runtimes to keep app size down: ML Drift acceleration is available now in the standalone LiteRT packages, but it's still "coming soon" to LiteRT in Google Play Services.

How to get started

The announcement gives two paths:

  • App developers: use the LiteRT ML Drift accelerator. You get model partitioning, tensor virtualization and LLM acceleration out of the box.
  • GPU and systems engineers: build directly on ML Drift's standalone C++ APIs from the GitHub repo to build custom GpuModel compute graphs and write your own shaders. There are quickstarts for OpenCL on Android and WebGPU via Dawn.

Source code: github.com/google-ai-edge/ml-drift. Issues and feature requests go on GitHub, and questions go to the Google AI Edge Community Forum.

The takeaway

If your app relies on the TFLite GPU delegate, it won't break today, but it's now frozen. Put a migration to the LiteRT ML Drift accelerator on your roadmap, benchmark your models before and after, and check the Play Services caveat if you ship an unbundled runtime.

Source: ML Drift: Next-Gen GPU AI/ML Inference at the Edge (Google Developers Blog)
